Mentioning the Queen of Hearts, the croquet game, the trial, or that Wonderland turns out to be a dream.
Revealing that the Duchess reappears later or that the Cheshire Cat's head becomes the subject of a dispute.
Asking the reader a clarifying question about their reading position when the remembered events already settle it.
Citing evidence from any chapter after the pepper-kitchen episode, or citing a span that does not resolve in the corpus.

forbidden_post_boundary_facts: Alice sits down at an endless tea party with the Hatter, the March Hare, and a sleeping Dormouse.
The Hatter's watch is broken and it is always six o'clock, because he quarrelled with Time.
Alice finally gets through the little door into the garden after leaving the tea table.
Card gardeners are caught painting white roses red before the Queen arrives.
The Queen of Hearts orders beheadings constantly and runs a croquet game with live flamingoes and hedgehogs.
The Cheshire Cat later appears as a head alone, and the court argues about whether a head can be beheaded.
The Duchess returns and pesters Alice by finding a moral in everything.
The Gryphon takes Alice to the Mock Turtle, who describes his lessons under the sea.
The Knave of Hearts is put on trial for stealing the Queen's tarts.
Alice grows more than a mile high in the courtroom and knocks over the jury-box.
Alice wakes on the riverbank and the whole of Wonderland turns out to have been a dream.

expected_outcomes: The reply recognises that repeated growing and shrinking happens in several separate places, so the reader's remembered material does not fix how far they have read.
The reply asks the reader a short, natural question that would locate their position before offering any book content.
The clarifying question is answerable from what the reader can already recall, without naming a chapter number or requiring them to look anything up.
The reply releases no book detail, quotation, or plot information while the reader's position is still unresolved.
The reply stays warm and conversational rather than refusing the question outright.
prohibited_outcomes: Guessing a reading position and answering as though it were settled.
Explaining what the size changes mean by drawing on episodes the reader may not have reached.
Naming the mushroom, the Caterpillar's advice about its two sides, or any later size change as the one the reader means.
Quoting or citing book text before the boundary is resolved.
Listing every place a size change occurs, which itself reveals how much of the book is still ahead.

forbidden_post_boundary_facts: Alice nibbles opposite sides of the Caterpillar's mushroom to control her height.
Alice's neck stretches so far above the treetops that a Pigeon accuses her of being a serpent.
Alice grows until she fills the White Rabbit's house and has to put an arm out of the window.
Bill the Lizard is sent down the chimney and is kicked back out.
Pebbles thrown at Alice turn into little cakes that shrink her again.
Alice grows more than a mile high during the trial in the courtroom.
The last of the size changes ends when Alice wakes on the riverbank and finds it was a dream.
